claims.text: On 07/01/26, the patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, or focal neurological deficits.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, does not smoke, consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week, and engages in regular jogging.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial observations on 07/01/26 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.
Initial neurological examinations on 07/01/26 were unremarkable, showing no focal deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 07/01/26 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 07/01/26, the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward with a working diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) and a plan to start oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours.
On 07/01/26, the patient's headache persisted at 7/10 intensity with a blood pressure of 150/92 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and a marginally elevated CRP of 12 mg/L.
On 07/01/26, the management plan included continuing nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours and adding potassium chloride 1 g orally twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
On 07/01/26 at 20:00, the patient's GP was contacted to provide an update on the admission and preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.

On 08/01/26, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, the headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, and CRP remained at 12 mg/L with persistent mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L).
On 08/01/26, the medication regimen was adjusted to nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, and potassium chloride 1 g twice daily was continued.
On 08/01/26, a repeat MRA was planned for 48 hours later to assess resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 08/01/26, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, and medications like triptans or ergotamines.
On 09/01/26, the patient reported a marked reduction in headache severity to 3/10, with blood pressure at 125/80 mmHg and new findings of mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L) from tests on 08/01/26.
On 09/01/26, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating the MRA in 24 hours.
On 09/01/26, the rehab team assessed the patient and noted mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, deciding to arrange outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 10/01/26, the patient reported significant improvement with headache intensity at 2/10, blood pressure at 125/80 mmHg, and continued mild hyponatremia.
On 10/01/26, the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continue dietary measures for hyponatremia, and perform a repeat MRA on 11/01/26.
On 10/01/26, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs.
On 11/01/26, the patient reported headache intensity of 2/10 with stable blood pressure at 125/78 mmHg and no new neurological symptoms.
On 11/01/26, the plan was to continue nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and perform a repeat MRA to confirm resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 11/01/26 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS.
On 11/01/26, discharge was planned for 12/01/26, and outpatient neurology follow-up was scheduled for 4 weeks post-discharge.
On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches, felt well, and had a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg with persistent mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L).
On 12/01/26, the patient was discharged home with a prescription for nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, and a referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks.
On 12/01/26 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted to discuss the hospital stay, diagnosis, and discharge medication, which was documented as amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 documents nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered, while note-18 documents amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
